buckets.Run And Persistence: These settings define run identity and local persistence behavior. They control where run artifacts are written and how configuration values are loaded and saved across calls. This bucket is used early in perforate_model before interactive target selection, so values here can change what defaults appear in the UI. If a value is manually set in code, that manual value is preserved over file-loaded values during the same process.
buckets.Target Selection: These settings decide what gets perforated, what gets tracked, and what gets transformed before wrapping. They are consumed by the model traversal and conversion logic that applies module and parameter rules. The UI writes into these lists during target selection, and recursive parent priority can make child-level overrides informational only. If you see mismatches between expected and applied behavior, this is the first bucket to inspect.
buckets.Switch Strategy: These settings control when the training loop decides to add or switch dendrite structure. They determine whether switching is fixed-interval, history-driven, always-on, or disabled. Most of these are read by the tracker and scheduling flow after perforation is initialized, not by the module selector itself. Tuning these values changes training dynamics and should be done with reproducibility in mind.
buckets.Optimization And Search: These settings govern score thresholds, retries, and search behavior after structural updates. They are used to decide whether a candidate change is accepted, retried, or rejected. Several values work together, so changing only one may have little effect unless related controls are adjusted too. Use this bucket when you want to tune convergence behavior rather than structural coverage.
buckets.Model Math: These settings affect numeric and shape-level behavior during perforation and training integration. They include dtype, device, and tensor size validation controls used across wrappers and runtime checks. Incorrect values here can cause subtle runtime issues even if selection rules are correct. Treat this bucket as low-level execution configuration.
buckets.Visualization And Logging: These settings control console verbosity and graph/test artifact output. They are read throughout training and tracking code paths, not just in the selector UI. If runs are noisy, slow, or writing too many files, this bucket usually contains the cause. These values do not usually change structural behavior directly.
buckets.Dashboard: These settings configure event emission and dashboard integration endpoints. They are consumed when emitting run lifecycle and update events. If dashboard output is missing or too verbose, adjust this bucket first. Keeping these values local makes it easier to isolate behavior per project.
buckets.Experimental: These settings expose behavior that is advanced, optional, or integration-specific. They may depend on external packages or less-traveled code paths. Because of that, defaults are usually conservative. Change these only when you know the downstream path that consumes them.
buckets.Other: Settings that do not map cleanly to another category appear here. They are still active global configuration values and may influence less common workflows. If you are unsure where a key belongs, inspect where it is read in the code and then consider rebucketing.

settings.save_name: save_name defines the run folder under the current working directory where run-scoped artifacts are stored. It is resolved and sanitized in perforate_model before initialization proceeds. The run config JSON path is derived from this value, so changing it changes where run-local configuration snapshots are written. If you want run-by-run records, this is the primary naming control.
settings.config_file: config_file is an optional pointer to a reusable local JSON configuration file. When set, it is loaded before run-specific config so it can provide baseline defaults for new runs. During the same process, manual code assignments still take priority and are not overwritten by file loads. If you want repeatable defaults across dated run folders, point this to a stable local file and set it before perforate_model.
settings.configuration_confirmed: This flag indicates whether interactive configuration has already been confirmed in the current process. perforate_model checks it to decide whether to open the target-selection UI. Setting it true can skip the selector, which is useful for scripted workflows with complete pre-configuration. It is a control-flow flag, not a model-behavior hyperparameter.
settings.module_names_to_perforate: This list applies perforation rules by module type name, such as Linear or Conv2d. It is consulted during module traversal and can affect many modules at once. In the selector UI this corresponds to name-level targeting and can be masked by higher-priority inherited parent decisions. Use this when you want broad class-level coverage quickly.
settings.module_ids_to_perforate: This list applies perforation to specific module paths using dot-notation IDs. It is the most direct way to target individual modules when class-wide rules are too broad. In nested structures, parent-priority inheritance can override child intent in effective behavior, which is surfaced in the UI markers. Prefer IDs when you need exact surgical control.
settings.module_names_to_track: This list tracks module types without perforating them. Tracking is used so modules are accounted for in the processing flow even when they are not transformed. This setting is useful for coverage accounting and compatibility passes. It is name-wide, so one entry can affect many modules.
settings.module_ids_to_track: This list tracks specific modules by ID without perforation. It is useful when you need fine-grained accounting or exclusion from transformation on a module-by-module basis. Like other child-level rules, effective behavior can be superseded by inherited parent priority in the current UI model. Use this when exact exceptions are required.
settings.parameter_ids_to_track: This list tracks individual parameters directly, separate from module-level rules. It is consumed when determining whether uncovered parameter paths should still be considered part of the managed set. This can be valuable for custom modules that expose standalone parameters. Keep IDs stable and dot-notated to avoid mismatches.
settings.switch_mode: switch_mode chooses which switching policy constant is active during training. Downstream tracker logic reads this to decide how and when to evaluate structural updates. It works in combination with n_epochs_to_switch, fixed_switch_num, and history parameters depending on selected mode. Changing switch_mode can dramatically change run behavior even with unchanged targets.
settings.n_epochs_to_switch: In history-based mode, this value acts like a patience window before triggering a switch consideration. It is evaluated against recent metric behavior managed by tracker state. Too small a value can cause over-eager switching and instability; too large can delay useful updates. Tune alongside history_lookback and thresholds.
settings.history_lookback: This defines the averaging window used by history-based switching logic. A larger window smooths noise but can hide short-term gains or regressions. A smaller window reacts quickly but is more sensitive to metric variance. It is most meaningful when switch_mode uses history criteria.
settings.fixed_switch_num: In fixed-switch mode, this sets the interval in epochs between switches. It is deterministic and ignores short-term metric fluctuations. This can simplify controlled experiments where timing consistency matters more than adaptive behavior. Use first_fixed_switch_num to delay only the first switch if needed.
settings.improvement_threshold: This list defines relative improvement thresholds, often interpreted by stage as dendrites are added. Tracker acceptance logic can compare candidate performance against these thresholds to decide whether updates are meaningful. Lower values increase sensitivity to small gains; higher values demand clearer wins. Keep list semantics consistent with your expected progression depth.
settings.improvement_threshold_raw: This value defines an absolute improvement floor used alongside or instead of relative thresholds. It protects against tiny numerical changes being treated as meaningful progress. In noisy metrics, raising this can reduce churn from marginal updates. In low-scale metrics, set carefully to avoid suppressing real gains.
settings.find_best_lr: When enabled, this allows learning-rate search behavior after structural changes. The goal is to recover or improve training stability when a new structure shifts optimization dynamics. It is not a universal win for every workload, but it often helps when post-switch behavior is brittle. Pair with dont_give_up_unless_learning_rate_lowered for stricter search persistence.
settings.dont_give_up_unless_learning_rate_lowere: This setting enforces at least one LR reduction path before abandoning search attempts. It helps avoid premature failure decisions when the current LR is simply too aggressive for the new structure. If disabled, search may terminate earlier with fewer fallback attempts. Use this when you want more resilient adaptation after updates.
settings.max_dendrite_tries: This caps retry attempts for candidate dendrite initialization before concluding a step is not improving. Increasing it can recover cases where random initialization quality is inconsistent. The tradeoff is additional compute and run time per decision point. Tune based on variance and cost tolerance.
settings.max_dendrites: This is a hard upper bound on how many dendrites can be added. It acts as a global safety and budget control regardless of switching policy. If performance still rises near the cap, you may be truncating potential gains. If runs become unstable before the cap, lower values can improve consistency.
settings.device: device controls where tensors and modules are expected to run, such as cpu or cuda. It influences allocation and execution paths throughout training and conversion. Mismatched device assumptions can produce runtime errors that look unrelated to configuration. Keep this aligned with environment and model placement.
settings.d_type: d_type defines the numeric dtype used for perforated weights and related tensors. It can influence memory usage, speed, and numerical stability. Mixed precision environments should verify this value is compatible with the rest of the training stack. Changing dtype can alter convergence characteristics.
settings.pai_forward_function: This is the activation function used by perforation components where applicable. It affects gradient shape and representational dynamics in those modules. Different functions may require retuning of optimization thresholds and learning rate behavior. Use a callable that is stable and well-understood for your model family.
settings.confirm_correct_sizes: When enabled, additional dimension checks are performed to validate tensor shape assumptions. This can catch configuration and wrapping mistakes earlier, especially in custom architectures. The tradeoff is some runtime overhead. It is a debugging aid, not a production speed setting.
settings.debugging_output_dimensions: This controls verbosity for tensor-dimension diagnostics. Higher levels typically expose more shape details that help isolate mismatch points. It is useful when integrating unusual module layouts or custom wrappers. Reduce it once the pipeline is stable to keep logs readable.
settings.verbose: verbose enables broader informational logging across the pipeline. It helps track control flow and configuration effects during experiments. In long runs it can produce substantial output volume. Use with extra_verbose and silent carefully to avoid conflicting expectations.
settings.extra_verbose: extra_verbose expands on verbose with additional low-level details. This is best used temporarily when diagnosing edge-case behavior. Continuous use can obscure key signals by flooding logs. Enable only while actively debugging.
settings.silent: silent suppresses most normal informational output. It is useful in automated contexts where logs should remain compact. Be aware that it can hide clues needed for troubleshooting configuration issues. Turn it off when debugging unexpected behavior.
settings.drawing_pai: This toggles standard graph generation associated with PAI training progress. Graph output is useful for diagnostics and reporting, but can add I/O overhead in large trial sweeps. If disabled, core training logic still runs but visualization artifacts are reduced. Keep enabled when interpreting run dynamics matters.
settings.drawing_extra_graphs: This enables additional graph outputs beyond the core set. These can provide deeper visibility but increase artifact volume and write time. In heavy experiment loops, disabling this can keep runs lighter. Use it when you need richer diagnostics.
settings.test_saves: test_saves controls whether extra intermediary test artifacts are written. It can be valuable during development but expensive in disk usage across many runs. This does not replace core run saves; it supplements them. Disable in large batch experiments unless needed.
settings.pai_saves: pai_saves enables PAI-specific save behavior intended for streamlined artifacts. It can reduce some scaffolding overhead in persisted outputs depending on flow. Ensure downstream loading paths expect this format choice. Treat it as an artifact-format policy setting.
settings.dashboard_events_enabled: This toggles emission of dashboard events during run lifecycle and updates. It is read where event emitters are invoked in initialization and training paths. Disabling it can reduce overhead and external dependencies in offline runs. Enable when live observability is required.
settings.dashboard_url: This is the dashboard endpoint used when event emission is enabled. Incorrect values can silently prevent expected updates from appearing. Keep it local and explicit per project to avoid accidental cross-environment routing. Verify connectivity when enabling dashboard output.
settings.learn_dendrites_live: This experimental flag enables advanced live dendrite learning behavior not typical in standard flows. It may rely on assumptions that are not active in every model or optimizer setup. Use only when you are intentionally evaluating that path. Expect to retune related strategy settings.
settings.perforated_backpropagation: This flag enables integration with perforated backpropagation when the external package is available. In this repository, that package is intentionally separate, so availability depends on environment setup. Keep false unless you explicitly installed and validated the dependency path. Turning it on without the package will not provide useful behavior.
settings.weight_tying_experimental: This controls experimental behavior around tied-weight handling. It is intended for specialized architectures where shared parameter semantics matter. Because tied weights can affect counting and update assumptions, validate thoroughly when enabled. Keep disabled unless your model design requires it.
